claims.text: Stable, coherent protective oxide layers form and persist above 900 °C when the oxygen chemical potential at the alloy surface is optimized.
Lower oxygen partial pressures produce an optimal oxide-growth rate.
A controlled oxide-growth rate minimizes internal stress and promotes adherent, coherent oxide scales.
Higher oxygen partial pressures accelerate oxide formation.
Accelerated oxide formation increases stress, cracking, and spallation.
SO2 or H2O modifies oxidation kinetics by changing diffusion rates and local reaction environments.
The proposed comparison varies oxygen partial pressure among 0.1, 0.2, and 0.5 atm O2 and independently adds controlled SO2 or H2O vapor.
The defined baseline is exposure at approximately 0.21 atm O2 without aggressive species.
The proposed exposure is at 950 °C for 50 to 150 hours.
Intermediary sub-oxides and changes in oxide-growth rate govern stress development and coherence at the oxide/alloy interface.
Oxygen chemical potential controls diffusion rates of Cr, Al, and Si toward the alloy surface.
Changes in reactive-element diffusion dictate the rate and nature of oxide-scale formation.
At optimized lower oxygen partial pressures, a thin, adherent, coherent scale with minimal cracking will form.
Al- or Si-enriched alloys will particularly favor formation of the predicted protective scale.
Higher oxygen partial pressures will produce thicker scales with substantial cracking and spallation.
The presence of additional corrosive species will produce thicker scales with substantial cracking and spallation.
The hypothesis applies to both single-phase and multiphase CrFeCoNiX metallic solid solutions around 950 °C over 50 to 150 hours.
Intrinsic grain size and diffusion pathways may affect oxidation independently of oxygen potential.
Comparable persistence and coherence of oxide scales at high and low oxygen partial pressures would falsify the proposed oxygen-potential effect.
